idiom_name: Stateless StateMachine<TState, TTrigger> with PermitIf guards + ASP.NET Core controller bridge
implementation_notes: In .NET the flow is usually modelled with the Stateless library: a StateMachine<State, Trigger> is configured per state with Permit(trigger, nextState) or PermitIf(trigger, nextState, guard), OnEntry/OnExit handlers run the command for each step, and the machine persists its state externally - StateMachine(typeof(State), typeof(Trigger), () => stored, s => stored = s) - so a conversation survives between requests. The ASP.NET Core controller action then only maps the incoming request to a trigger, fires it and returns the view or redirect that the machine selected. What replaces the classic structure is that configured machine plus the framework's controller pipeline: the command objects become trigger-triggered handlers and the view references become IActionResult or route names. Hand-write the classic Application Controller with its own command classes when the flow must be driven from several front ends or the state model is richer than a flat machine; Windows Workflow Foundation's StateMachine activity is the legacy in-box alternative and is no longer a .NET Core option.
pitfalls: A StateMachine instance is not thread-safe for concurrent Fire calls: a double submit or two tabs can both read the stored state and interleave transitions, so the persisted state needs an optimistic-concurrency check (a version or ETag alongside it).
PermitIf guards are evaluated on every attempted transition, including attempts that are then rejected: keep them pure reads, or side effects fire on illegal transitions too.

ASP.NET Core's Controller/ControllerBase is the Page Controller of MVC; expecting it to own cross-screen flow re-creates exactly the duplication this pattern removes - keep the machine (or flow service) as the single decision point.
